learningObjectives: Explain the two-process model of sleep timing.
Identify major circadian and sleep-wake control structures.
Recognise how sleep disruption affects psychological assessment.

anatomy.label: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
anatomy.detail: Uses retinal light input to synchronise daily rhythms.
anatomy.clinical: Misalignment can produce delayed or irregular sleep timing.

anatomy.label: Ventrolateral preoptic area
anatomy.detail: Inhibits arousal systems to permit stable sleep.
anatomy.clinical: Reduced sleep drive or competing arousal can fragment sleep.

anatomy.label: Orexin system
anatomy.detail: Lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons prevent abrupt state switching.
anatomy.clinical: Loss of orexin is central to narcolepsy type 1.

anatomy.label: Ascending arousal system
anatomy.detail: Cholinergic and monoaminergic nuclei support wake and REM transitions.
anatomy.clinical: Medication and neurological disease can disrupt state control.

anatomy.label: Thalamocortical loops
anatomy.detail: Coordinate oscillatory NREM activity and sensory gating.
anatomy.clinical: Fragmentation may reduce restorative and memory-related processes.

stages.label: Light cue
stages.text: Retinal input adjusts the circadian clock.

stages.label: Cycle
stages.text: NREM and REM stages alternate through the night.

stages.label: Reset
stages.text: Morning light and activity reinforce the next circadian cycle.

quizBank.question: Sleep timing is governed mainly by interaction between:
quizBank.explanation: The two-process model combines circadian timing with accumulated sleep pressure.

quizBank.question: The suprachiasmatic nucleus primarily:
quizBank.explanation: The SCN is the central circadian pacemaker.

quizBank.question: Orexin helps:
quizBank.explanation: Orexin prevents unstable transitions between sleep and wake.

quizBank.question: Sleep spindles occur mainly during:
quizBank.explanation: Spindles are characteristic thalamocortical NREM oscillations.

quizBank.question: A client who cannot sleep at 10 pm but sleeps normally from 2 am to 10 am may have:
quizBank.explanation: Normal sleep at a delayed biological time suggests circadian misalignment rather than global inability to sleep.

reviewPrompts: Sleep timing is governed mainly by interaction between:
Ask when the person can sleep, not only whether they can sleep. Circadian misalignment and insomnia require different formulations.
